## Three ways to combine models

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Chained**

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'rankSpacing': 32}}}%%
flowchart TB
  d["Data A"] --> m1["Model 1"]
  m1 --> e["Summary"]
  e --> m2["Model 2"]
  m2 --> a["Answer"]
```

Uncertainty is approximated at each hand-off, and that biases the
result.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Joint**

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'rankSpacing': 32}}}%%
flowchart TB
  a["Data A"] --> m
  b["Data B"] --> m
  c["Data C"] --> m["One model"]
  m --> o["Answer"]
```

Rigorous, and nobody can take it apart. England's COVID-19 models were
not adapted to mpox in 2022.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**Composable**

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'rankSpacing': 32}}}%%
flowchart TB
  lib[("Existing parts")] --> p1["Infection"]
  lib --> p2["Latent"]
  lib --> p3["Observation"]
  p1 --> f["Fit together"]
  p2 --> f
  p3 --> f
  f --> o["Answer"]
```

Each part checked on its own. The parts have to exist. Mostly they do
not.
:::
::::

::: {.callout-important}
Modelling evidence has to be timely, rigorous, and collaborative. Most
approaches manage two of the three.
:::

::: {.attribution}
Schematics, not measured results · Criteria, Whitty (2015),
[doi:10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8) ·
Joint model, Birrell et al. (2025),
[doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030](https://doi.org/10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf030) ·
Mpox, Endo et al. (2022),
[doi:10.1126/science.add4507](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add4507) ·
Chaining bias, Lison et al. (2024),
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021)
:::

## Chaining models loses information

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- The ONS COVID-19 Infection Survey tested over four million swabs from
  more than 150,000 households at a cost above £500 million. Modellers
  outside saw the published prevalence, not the swabs
- Prevalence fed incidence and $R_t$, and those fed variant
  transmissibility and severity
- Uncertainty was approximated at each step and assumptions were
  inherited unchecked
- Chaining steps like these can bias the result and understate the
  uncertainty

::: {.callout-important}
Joint fitting is the fix, and it hands you a model nobody can take
apart.
:::
:::

## So everyone rebuilds the whole model

- At least seven packages estimate $R_t$ by renewal in Stan. Only two
  of them share any component, and I wrote both
- The wastewater $R_t$ tools make different choices about how much of
  the sampling to represent, and share nothing. It is not clear which
  of those choices matter
- Shared parts do exist. `primarycensored` is one, and uptake outside
  my own packages is thin

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'rankSpacing': 32}}}%%
flowchart TB
  epidemia["epidemia"]
  epimap["epimap"]
  epiline["epiline"]
  EpiSewer["EpiSewer"]
  wwinference["wwinference"]
  EpiNow2["EpiNow2"] --> pc(["primarycensored.stan"])
  epinowcast["epinowcast"] --> pc
```

::: {.attribution}
Seven packages, and every component any of them share. The arrows are
`primarycensored.stan`, vendored by `EpiNow2` and `epinowcast`
:::
